content: Oral 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) was developed to retain the therapeutic benefits of sulfasalazine (SASP) while minimizing its adverse effects. Previous research has shown that 5-ASA at doses of at least 2 g/day is more effective than placebo in inducing remission in ulcerative colitis (UC), but it is not more effective than SASP. This updated review aimed to evaluate the efficacy, dose-response relationship, and safety of oral 5-ASA compared to placebo, SASP, or other 5-ASA formulations. Additionally, it sought to compare the effectiveness and safety of once-daily dosing of 5-ASA with conventional dosing regimens (two or three times daily). The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults with active UC. Studies comparing oral 5-ASA with placebo, SASP, or other 5-ASA formulations were included, as well as those comparing once-daily dosing with conventional dosing and dose-ranging studies. The outcomes assessed included failure to achieve clinical remission, clinical improvement, endoscopic remission, endoscopic improvement, adherence to treatment, adverse events (AEs), serious adverse events (SAEs), and withdrawals due to AEs. A total of 54 studies involving 9,612 participants were included in the analysis. Most studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias. Among participants receiving 5-ASA, 71% failed to achieve clinical remission compared to 83% of those receiving placebo, indicating that 5-ASA is more effective than placebo (risk ratio [RR] 0.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.82 to 0.89; high-certainty evidence). A dose-response trend was observed for 5-ASA, with higher doses being more effective. However, there was no significant difference in clinical remission rates between 5-ASA and SASP. Specifically, 54% of participants receiving 5-ASA failed to achieve remission compared to 58% of those receiving SASP (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.04; moderate-certainty evidence). When comparing once-daily dosing with conventional dosing, there was no significant difference in clinical remission rates. Sixty percent of participants receiving once-daily dosing failed to achieve remission compared to 61% of those on conventional dosing (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.06; high-certainty evidence). Adherence rates were also similar, with 8% of once-daily participants failing to adhere to their regimen compared to 6% of conventionally dosed participants (RR 1.36, 95% CI 0.64 to 2.86; low-certainty evidence). There was no evidence of a difference in efficacy among various 5-ASA formulations. Fifty percent of participants receiving one 5-ASA formulation failed to achieve remission compared to 52% of those receiving a comparator 5-ASA formulation (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.02; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the incidence of adverse events or serious adverse events between 5-ASA and placebo, once-daily and conventional dosing, or different 5-ASA formulations. Common adverse events included flatulence, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, and worsening of UC symptoms. SASP was less well-tolerated than 5-ASA. Twenty-nine percent of participants receiving SASP experienced adverse events compared to 15% of those receiving 5-ASA (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.63; moderate-certainty evidence). In conclusion, there is high-certainty evidence that 5-ASA is more effective than placebo for inducing remission in UC, but moderate-certainty evidence suggests it is not more effective than SASP. Given the relative costs, there appears to be no clear clinical advantage to using 5-ASA over SASP. High-certainty evidence indicates that once-daily dosing of 5-ASA is as effective as conventional dosing. Additionally, there appears to be little or no difference in efficacy or safety among the various 5-ASA formulations.
